title: Vowel letters, syllables and stress

objectives.can: Read ה, ו and י as vowel letters where they are, divide a word into syllables and find its stress.

explanation.summary: Three letters, ו י ה, sometimes stand for a vowel instead of a consonant. Knowing when they do, how a word divides into syllables and which syllable carries the stress lets you read a pointed word aloud.

sections.heading: Letters that stand for vowels
body: The old consonantal text had no vowel points, but the letters ו י ה (and rarely א) came to be used to hint at a vowel. The school name for such a letter is mater lectionis ('mother of reading'); in the plural, matres lectionis. The Masoretes later added the points. In a pointed word you read the point and the vowel letter together: the letter is silent in its own right and lengthens or marks the vowel.

ו can show o or u. With a holem above it (as in טוֹב) it shows o; with a dot inside it (as in רוּחַ) it shows u. י can show i or e: after a hireq it shows i (as in the י of אֱלֹהִים), and after a tsere or a segol it shows e (as in בֵּין). A ה at the end of a word can show a, e or o; in לָיְלָה it only shows the vowel ā before it and is silent. The א is sometimes silent as well, as in בָּרָא, where it rests after the vowel.

These letters are not always vowel letters. Each of them is also a real consonant. The י of יוֹם and the ו at the start of וַיֹּאמֶר are consonants, and so is a ה that carries a mappiq. A ו or י is a vowel letter when it stands after the point it goes with (a holem before ו, a hireq or tsere before י) or when it carries the dot of a shureq. At the start of a word, or when it has a vowel of its own, it is a consonant.

sections.heading: Full and defective spelling
body: The same word can be written with a vowel letter or without one. The spelling with the vowel letter is called plene ('full') and the spelling without it defective. The reading is the same. The name David is written דָּוִד in the book of Kings and דָּוִיד in Chronicles: the vowel is the same and the י only marks it. Do not look for a difference of meaning in such pairs. They are one word with two spellings.

sections.heading: Syllables
body: A Hebrew syllable begins with a consonant and has exactly one vowel. (The one exception is the conjunction וּ, 'and', before certain letters, which is itself a vowel.) A syllable that ends in a vowel is open; one that ends in a consonant is closed. In בָּרָא there are two open syllables, ba and ra. In אוֹר there is one closed syllable. In בְּרֵאשִׁית there are three syllables, with the shewa as a short vowel on the first.

A silent shewa closes a syllable and a vocal shewa starts one; the lesson on shewa gave the rules. A dagesh forte splits its letter between two syllables: הַשָּׁמַיִם is read hash-sha-ma-yim, and its first syllable is closed by the first half of the doubled ש.

Long vowels tend to stand in open syllables or in the stressed syllable. Short vowels tend to stand in closed syllables that are not stressed. Grammarians state the rules differently and they have exceptions; the traditional school rule is only a guide.

sections.heading: Stress
body: In most Hebrew words the stress falls on the last syllable, as in בְּרֵאשִׁית (be-re-SHIT), בָּרָא (ba-RA) and אֱלֹהִים (e-lo-HIM). In a good number of words it falls on the syllable before the last. These include nouns of the pattern of מֶלֶךְ, 'king', which is read ME-lekh, and of אֶרֶץ, 'earth', and words such as לָיְלָה (LAY-la) and הַשָּׁמַיִם (hash-sha-MA-yim).

In a printed Hebrew Bible the stress is marked by the accent sign written on or by the stressed syllable. The signs also divide the verse and were used for chant; the next lesson says more. Only when you know where the accent is can you read the vowels correctly, because a vowel often changes when the stress moves.

misunderstandings: A ו, י or ה is not always a vowel letter. At the start of a word, or when a vowel follows it, it is a consonant.
A plene and a defective spelling are not two words. They are one word, spelled with and without a vowel letter.
The stress is not always on the last syllable, and it is not always on the one before. Learn the patterns.
A dagesh forte divides a syllable. The doubled letter ends one syllable and begins the next.
The accent sign is not a vowel. It is written beside the vowel and marks the stressed syllable.

deeper.heading: Why there are vowel letters at all
body: Hebrew was written for centuries with consonants only, and readers supplied the vowels. Scribes began to use ו י ה to make hard words clear, and they spread them unevenly. That is why the same word can be spelled in more than one way, and why spelling in the late books of the Bible has more vowel letters than in the early ones. The Masoretes preserved each book's spelling and added the points above, below and inside the letters.

quoted.english: And God called the light Day, and the darkness He called Night. And there was evening and there was morning, one day.

examples.analysis: יוֹם begins with a consonant י; the ו after the holem is a vowel letter for o, and the word is one closed syllable. לָיְלָה has two syllables, lay and la; the final ה is a vowel letter and is silent, and the accent stands on the first syllable, so the stress is early in the word.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בְּרֵאשִׁית is read be-re-SHIT, three syllables, with the stress on the last: the accent stands on the final syllable. The א in it is silent, resting after the tsere, and the י is a vowel letter for i. אֱלֹהִים has a י for i and the stress on the last syllable. הַשָּׁמַיִם is read hash-sha-MA-yim: the doubled ש splits across two syllables and the stress is on the syllable before the last.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: תֹהוּ and רוּחַ both have the long vowel u written with a shureq, the ו with a dot inside. In תֹהוּ the other vowel, o, is a holem with no vowel letter at all: a defective spelling of o beside a full spelling of u.
